Populations of the serrasalmid Pacu (Prosomyleus rhomboidalis) inhabiting the Amazon basin exhibit a maximum standard length that is among the largest recorded for frugivorous characiforms. Extensive mark-recapture surveys in the lower Tocantins River indicate that individuals ultimately attain an asymptotic size of 40.7 centimeters [Li = 40.7 centimeters], a value derived from longitudinal growth trajectories of adult fish. This ultimate length appears to be constrained by the energetic demands of seasonal fruit pulses, which drive somatic growth primarily during the flood pulse. In contrast, the standard length at which reproductive maturation is initiated is considerably smaller; histological analysis of gonadal tissue from fish collected during the rising-water period revealed that the onset of gametogenesis occurs at a body size of 15 centimeters [Lp = 15 centimeters]. This size threshold is reached within the first two to three years of life, depending on local resource availability, and marks a clear transition from a strictly somatic growth phase to one integrating both growth and gonadal investment. The disparity between size at puberty and ultimate length underscores a prolonged adult growth phase, a life-history strategy common among large-bodied characins that face size-dependent predation risk and variable food abundance.

Under the thermal conditions of the pre-flood period, at a water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], gravid females displayed a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 20% [GSI = 20%]. This value indicates that nearly one-fifth of a female's total body mass is dedicated to ovarian tissue at the moment of spawning, a relatively high reproductive investment consistent with the production of numerous small, pelagic eggs. The index was calculated from dissected ovaries of fish captured during November and December, and it exhibited relatively low inter-individual variation, suggesting a synchronized spawning strategy aligned with the onset of the annual flood cycle. This energetic commitment to egg production is notable given the frugivorous diet of the species, which may impose seasonal constraints on lipid accumulation. The gonadosomatic index was 20% [GSI = 20%] at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C].

Larval development in Pacu proceeds rapidly once the eggs have been fertilized and released into the warm, productive waters of the floodplain. Field observations of captive-spawned egg batches maintained in outdoor rearing enclosures under ambient river temperatures demonstrated that eclosion occurs after a brief incubation period. When water temperatures were held at a constant 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the age at birth, defined as the moment of chorion rupture and the emergence of the yolk-sac larva, was recorded at 9.5 days [ab = 9.5 days]. This developmental rate is typical for tropical characids spawning during the warm rainy season and is facilitated by the elevated metabolic rates associated with these thermal conditions. The newly emerged prolarvae are extremely small and transparent, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves for their initial nutrition. The transition from the yolk-sac stage to first exogenous feeding follows within a few days, as the mouth opens and the digestive tract becomes functional. The rapidity of this embryonic period, at 9.5 days [ab = 9.5 days], is an adaptation that minimizes the time the developing embryo is exposed to benthic egg predators during incubation on submerged vegetation at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C].

The wet weight of a newly hatched Pacu larva at the moment of emergence is remarkably low, reflecting the species' strategy of producing large numbers of small offspring. Based on the measured egg diameter of 1.6 millimeters, which corresponds to a calculated spherical volume, the estimated wet weight at birth is 0.0021 grams [Wwb = 0.0021 grams]. This minuscule body mass places the newly emerged prolarva among the smallest of the Serrasalmidae and imposes an immediate necessity for efficient yolk utilization and rapid development of feeding structures. In stark contrast, the maximum wet weight attained by a fully grown adult in the wild is several orders of magnitude greater. Analysis of the length-weight relationship derived from a large sample of adults from the lower Amazon, using the equation 0.02089 times the standard length raised to the power of 2.96, predicts a maximum wet weight of 1300 grams [Wwi = 1300 grams]. This remarkable increase in mass, spanning nearly six orders of magnitude from the neonatal stage to the largest recorded adult, exemplifies an extreme ontogenetic trajectory. The conversion of initial egg reserves into the somatic and gonadal tissues of a mature fish requires effective foraging on seasonal fruit falls and efficient assimilation of plant-derived carbohydrates and proteins.

Longevity data for Prosomyleus rhomboidalis, primarily derived from recaptures of individually tagged fish in a long-term study within a floodplain lake system, indicate a relatively extended lifespan for a tropical characin. Individuals maintained under stable conditions in captivity, or those experiencing low fishing pressure in protected areas, have been documented to survive for a maximum of 2920 days [am = 2920 days], which is the equivalent of eight years at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This maximum recorded lifespan is positively correlated with the attainment of the ultimate standard length of 40.7 centimeters [Li = 40.7 centimeters], suggesting that individuals who achieve the asymptotic size also enjoy the longest survival. However, it is important to note that this longevity value of 2920 days [am = 2920 days] was recorded at the same water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C] that also governs the rapid early development of the species. This apparent contradiction, where high metabolic temperatures support both rapid growth to a large size and a long lifespan, may be resolved by the seasonal food limitation that slows somatic growth in the wild, effectively decoupling the metabolic clock from chronological age. Natural mortality in older fish is typically attributed to piscivorous predators, such as river dolphins and large catfish, rather than to intrinsic senescence, and the oldest recorded individuals are often those occupying deep-channel refugia during the dry season.
